summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered 1600 through 1699, published as a status report. It gives each RFC's author, date, title and abstract, and marks those on the standards track. It is a reference index rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents for one hundred of the internet's instruction booklets, with a short blurb for each.

subtitle: An annotated index of 100 RFCs published between 1994 and 1997, organized by number with abstracts.

tldr.problem: The RFC series has grown large and it is hard to keep track of what has been published, especially across a numbered range.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a single document listing each RFC from 1600 through 1699, including the author, publication date, title, and a short abstract of each.
tldr.outcome: Readers get a quick reference to 100 RFCs in one place, with notes about which are on the standards track. This is not a protocol but a finding aid and status report.

today: RFC 1699 is an informational status report documenting the RFCs published in the 1600s range. It is itself not a standard and has never been obsoleted. It serves as a historical snapshot of Internet development during a period of rapid growth and intense discussion about the next generation of IP. Later RFC series now have their own summary documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC is a slightly annotated list of the RFCs numbered 1600 through 1699. It serves as a status report on these 100 RFCs, providing an index that helps readers quickly identify which RFCs cover which topics.

Each entry includes the RFC number, author, publication month and year, title, and a brief abstract or summary. RFCs on the standards track (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, or Internet Standard) are marked with [STANDARDS-TRACK]. The document notes that the status of RFCs may change over time, so readers should consult the current edition of Internet Official Protocol Standards for the authoritative status.
sections.plainLanguage: When a library gets new books, it publishes a list showing what each book is about. This is that list for 100 instruction books.

sections.title: The Range: RFCs 1600–1699
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs covered span from October 1994 (RFC 1698) through January 1997 (RFC 1699 itself). They reflect the rapid growth of the Internet during the mid-1990s. The range includes a mix of standards-track specifications, experimental protocols, and informational documents covering areas such as:

  • Internet Protocol Next Generation (IPng): Multiple RFCs proposing and analyzing IPng candidates, addressing concerns from different perspectives (corporate networks, cellular, cable TV, military, research, etc.).
  • Management Information Base (MIB) and network management: SNMPv2, MIBs for Ethernet, ATM, modem, and various devices.
  • Email and messaging: SMTP extensions, X.400 mapping, Unicode in MIME.
  • Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP): Various PPP variants and control protocols.
  • Routing and addressing: BGP-4, NAT, NSAP allocation.
  • Directory services: X.500 implementations and guidelines.
  • Other protocols and services: DNS, FTP, Telnet, virtual terminals, and many more.
sections.plainLanguage: This period was when the Internet was growing fast, and a lot of new ideas were being written down. The list shows 100 different ideas: some about addresses, some about mail, some about managing networks.

sections.title: Standards-Track RFCs
sections.content:
Many of the RFCs in this range are on the standards track, meaning they are under consideration for standardization. Notable standards-track RFCs include:

  • RFC 1654–1655, 1657: BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol version 4) specifications and implementation experience.
  • RFC 1651–1653: SMTP Service Extensions (framework and specific extensions for message size and 8-bit MIME transport).
  • RFC 1638: PPP Bridging Control Protocol.
  • RFC 1618–1619, 1662–1663: PPP variants (ISDN, SONET/SDH, reliable transmission, HDLC-like framing).
  • RFC 1650, 1623, 1643, 1658–1660: Definitions of managed objects for various device types using SMIv2.
  • RFC 1626, 1629: IP MTU for ATM AAL5 and NSAP allocation guidelines.

The standards track reflects the work of IETF working groups on core Internet protocols and management infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the 100 are official rules that the Internet community is agreeing to use. They are marked with a note saying 'this is becoming official'.

sections.title: Informational and Experimental RFCs
sections.content:
The majority of RFCs in this range are informational or experimental. They include:

  • IPng white papers (RFC 1675–1688, 1705–1707): Multiple positions on IPv6 selection, security, transition, corporate needs, mobility, and related concerns.
  • Process documents: RFC 1610 (Internet Official Protocol Standards), RFC 1636 (IAB security workshop report), RFC 1640 (POISED working group summary).
  • Protocol proposals: RFC 1693 (Partial Order Service for TCP), RFC 1692 (TMux), RFC 1644 (T/TCP), RFC 1705 (TCPng proposal).
  • Directory and naming: RFC 1632 (X.500 catalog), RFC 1617, 1625 (X.500 and WAIS).
  • User guides and reports: RFC 1635 (How to Use Anonymous FTP), RFC 1631 (NAT), RFC 1689 (Networked Information Retrieval tools).

These documents capture discussions, proposals, surveys, and analyses that shaped Internet development but do not mandate standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Many of the others are 'let's talk about this' documents—ideas, surveys, and discussions that help people think about what to do next.
